land.text: Volhynia, given to Igor in the division of Yaroslav's lands (the rus dossier, Kievan Rus' page); Cliopatria's first Volhynia shape is 1056

predecessors.note: The Volhynia page's infobox names Kievan Rus' and Yotvingia as predecessors and gives 'Established: 987' (founded by the Rurikid prince Vsevolod in 987); the map starts the state at the 1054 division because the rus dossier ends then.

land.text: Volhynia, united with Halych under Roman Mstislavich in 1199 (Roman the Great page)

successors.note: The Roman page: 'In 1199, after the death of Prince Volodymyr Yaroslavych of Halych' Roman took the Galician throne and created the Principality of Galicia-Volhynia. Cliopatria keeps the Volhynia row to 1201 and starts Galicia-Volhynia in 1202.

capitals.name: Volodymyr (Volodymyr-Volynskyi)
capitals.note: Infobox capital 'Volodymyr'. The page says that from 1154 to 1199 the principality was referred to as the Principality of Volodymyr, when Lutsk (1154-1228) was separated. Coordinates are the modern town.

correction.text: the 1056 shape, assumed for 1054-1055: western Volhynia with Volodymyr, Lutsk, Belz, Chelm and Kovel and, to the north, Brest, Lida and Grodno

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the Volhynia page gives no date for the 1054 division and no extent; the keyframe bridges the rus dossier's 1054 hand-over (Kievan Rus' ends 20 February 1054 there) to Cliopatria's first Volhynia shape in 1056 and assumes the 1056 shape. Confidence of the shape: 1.

82,372 km2 for 1056-1191. The infobox of the page gives no area, so no ratio can be taken. The page puts the Izyaslavichi of Turov on Volhynia from 1069 to 1118 and dates no frontier before the 1154 separation of Lutsk, so the shape stands unverified. The gazetteer puts Volodymyr, Lutsk, Belz, Chelm, Kovel, Brest, Lida and Grodno inside it and Dubno and Zhytomyr outside, so it covers Berestye and the Grodno lands rather than the eastern Volhynia of Dubno; no page opened says which towns belonged to the principality.

correction.text: the same shape for 1192-1199 only; from 1199 the land belongs to the Principality of Galicia-Volhynia

keyframe_review.note: 82,371 km2, the 1056 shape unchanged (351 cells both). The years are corrected only: Roman united Halych and Volhynia in 1199 ('In 1199, after the death of Prince Volodymyr Yaroslavych of Halych' Roman took the Galician throne), so Volhynia as a separate state ends in 1199, not 1201.

region.text: Volhynia as Cliopatria draws it from 1056

ledger.note: 1054: Volhynia is a principality of its own, the share of Yaroslav's son Igor. The Volhynia page's list of princes has 'Igor Yaroslavich (1054-1057)', then Rostislav of Tmutarakan (1057-1064); it gives 'Established: 987' ('founded by the Rurikid prince Vsevolod in 987') and no boundary for 1054, so the land is Cliopatria's 1056 shape. [Reviewer eu-16-c: confidence raised from 1, the year is on the page's list of princes.]

1069: Volhynia passes to the Izyaslavichi. The page: 'From 1069 to 1118, it belonged to the Izyaslavichi who primarily ruled from Turov'; 'After losing Turov to the Monomakhovichi in 1105' the line kept Volhynia. A change of ruling house on the same land; no border moves.

region.text: the Principality of Lutsk (1154-1228), separated from Volodymyr

ledger.note: 1154: the Principality of Lutsk is separated from Volhynia, which is then called the Principality of Volodymyr (1154-1199). The page: 'From 1154 to 1199, the Principality was referred to as the Principality of Volodymyr' 'when the Principality of Lutsk (1154–1228) was separated.' Cliopatria keeps Lutsk inside the Volhynia shape throughout.

region.text: Halych, taken by Roman in 1188 after the death of Yaroslav Osmomysl

ledger.note: 1188: Roman Mstislavich takes Halych from Volodymyr. The Roman page: 'Roman captured Halych, but was soon expelled by Hungarian king Bela III'; his brother Vsevolod took his seat at Volodymyr meanwhile.
1188: Roman is expelled from Halych by Bela III of Hungary, the same year he took it ('soon expelled'); the page gives no month.

1199: Halych and Volhynia are united under Roman. 'In 1199, after the death of Prince Volodymyr Yaroslavych of Halych,' Roman took the Galician throne a second time, creating the Principality of Galicia-Volhynia. Volhynia is absorbed into it.

region.text: Volhynia, as Cliopatria draws it to 1201

ledger.note: 1199: Volhynia ends as a separate principality in the union with Halych under Roman Mstislavich; his death in 1205 at Zawichost began the 'War of the Galician Succession (1205-1245)'. Cliopatria carries the row to 1201.

wars.name: Roman Mstislavich's campaigns for Halych
wars.outcome: Roman took Halych in 1188 and was soon expelled by Bela III; he took the Galician throne again in 1199 and united Halych and Volhynia.
wars.note: The Roman page gives 1188 and 1199 only; the years between (his 1196 war against his father-in-law Rurik with the Olgovichi) concern Kiev, not Volhynian frontiers.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line is on the pages opened; the frontier with Poland, Halych and the Yotvingians is approximate throughout.

sources.title: Principality of Volhynia
sources.note: Infobox (capital Volodymyr, 'Established 987', predecessor Kievan Rus' and Yotvingia), the Izyaslavichi 1069-1118, Lutsk separated 1154, the union with Halych in 1199. No area, no frontier.

sources.title: Roman the Great
sources.note: 1170 Volodymyr, 1188 Halych taken and lost, 1199 union of Halych and Volhynia, 1205 death at Zawichost.

notes: Two pages opened (budget 1-2). Start 1054 and the new keyframe 1054-1055 follow the rus dossier (it hands Volhynia to Igor on the death of Yaroslav in 1054, with Cliopatria's first Volhynia shape in 1056); the Volhynia page itself says 'Established 987'. End 1199 follows the Roman page; Cliopatria and the Halych row run to 1201 and principality-of-galicia-volhynia (already written) starts in 1199, so the two overlap by the one year of the union. Principality of Lutsk (1154-1228) needs a dossier if the project wants it (suggested slug principality-of-lutsk; Cliopatria has no row). The Cliopatria shape reaches Brest, Lida and Grodno (Berestye) and misses Dubno and Zhytomyr; the pages opened do not settle which towns were Volhynian.
